transcript.text: keep getting a little tingle off the washing machine when i touch the top of it while its on. is that normal?? its a indesit

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using it now. If you can do it safely, switch it off at the socket or at the consumer unit (fuse box). A shock usually means an earth or insulation fault, so don't use it again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has found and fixed it. No, that isn't normal. A tingle from the casing means electricity is reaching the metal body, and that must never happen. Please unplug it at the wall and don't use it again until a qualified engineer or electrician has checked it. The most likely causes, in order:
1. A broken or missing earth. All washing machines leak a tiny amount of current to the casing through their interference filter. Normally the earth wire carries it away safely. If the earth isn't connected, you feel it as a tingle. Common culprits are a faulty socket, an old or cheap extension lead or adaptor, a damaged plug, or a loose earth lead inside the machine.
2. Leakage inside the machine. The heater element is the classic one: as it ages, its insulation breaks down. Water dripping onto wiring or the motor can do the same. This kind of leak usually shows up more when the machine is heating or after a leak.
3. A damaged mains lead or plug, for example one crushed behind the machine. What you can safely check with it unplugged and without touching anything inside:
1. How it's plugged in. If it runs through an extension lead or adaptor, that's a strong suspect for a lost earth. Don't use that lead for anything else until it's checked.
2. Look at the plug and lead. Signs of scorching, melting, cracks or a crushed section point to the lead or plug.
3. Look under and around the machine for any water or damp marks. Signs of a leak make water on the electrics more likely.
4. Think about whether your fuse box trip switch has tripped recently. RCD trips alongside the tingle point more towards leakage inside the machine, like the heater. Whatever those show, the next step is a proper electrical test. An electrician can test the socket's earth. An appliance engineer can do an earth and insulation test on the machine itself, which pinpoints whether it's the earth lead, heater or something else. A heater element or earth lead repair is usually well worth doing on a machine that's otherwise fine. Is it plugged straight into the wall, or through an extension or adaptor? And has the trip switch ever gone while it's running?
its on a four way extension lead, the dryer is on it too cos the wall socket is behind the dryer. nothing has tripped no. its only a tingle though

⚠ Stop using this appliance
I know it's only a tingle, but please don't let that reassure you. A mild tingle usually means the earth isn't doing its job. The earth is the safety path that would carry a fault away. If something then fails inside, such as the heater, the full mains voltage can sit on the metal casing with nothing to stop it. That's when a tingle becomes a dangerous shock, especially with wet hands. So it stays off until it's been tested. 1. Most likely, a lost earth in the extension lead, its plug or the wall socket. The normal tiny leakage has nowhere to go, but it's too small to trip anything.
2. Next, an earth fault in the machine itself, either its internal earth lead or its mains lead or plug.
3. Less likely, leakage from inside the machine, such as the heater element. That kind of fault often trips the RCD sooner or later, but not always. The extension lead is a concern for another reason too. A washing machine and a tumble dryer can each draw close to the full 13 amps a four-way lead is rated for. Running both on one lead can overload it, and that's a common cause of overheating, scorched plugs and fires. Whatever the outcome, they shouldn't share a lead. Ideally each should have its own wall socket, and an electrician can add or move one so it isn't hidden behind the dryer. 1. Look closely at the extension lead's sockets, its plug and both appliance plugs. Brown or scorch marks, melted plastic, or a plug that has felt warm in use point strongly at the lead or socket. Stop using that lead completely if you see any.
2. Think about whether you've ever felt a tingle off the dryer too. If both tingle, the shared lead or the wall socket is probably the problem. If it's only the washer, the machine's own earth or lead becomes more likely. Please don't try the washer in another socket to see if the tingle goes away. It needs testing before it's used again either way. An electrician can test the socket and replace the lead setup. An appliance engineer can earth- and insulation-test the machine, which tells you for certain whether the machine itself is at fault. Have you ever noticed it from the dryer, or any marks or heat on the lead or plugs?

not sure about the dryer, never noticed. the plug does look a bit scorched near one pin now you say, and the lead has been trapped under the machines foot. theres also a sink right next to it and i'm usually barefoot on the tiles when i feel it

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Those three details change the picture quite a bit, and they make it more serious, not less. The scorch mark and the trapped lead now look like the most likely causes:
1. The crushed lead. A mains lead pinned under a machine's foot gets squashed and flexed every time the machine vibrates on spin. That can break the earth wire inside, which would explain the tingle. It can also damage the insulation around the live wire, which is worse.
2. The scorched plug. Scorching beside a pin means that connection has been overheating. That's typical of a loose or worn contact, and of an extension lead carrying a washer and a dryer together. A connection that is overheating can also be one that is losing its earth.
3. Internal leakage, such as the heater, is now a distant third. There's an obvious external cause, and nothing has tripped. Being barefoot on tiles next to a sink matters too. Your bare feet on a floor that may be damp give the current a very good path through you. That's why you feel what someone in shoes might not. It also means that if the fault got worse, you would get the full force of it. Please don't touch it barefoot again, even switched off, until it's been sorted. With everything unplugged, there are a few safe things you can look at:
1. Work out which plug is scorched. If it's the washing machine's own plug, the machine's lead and plug need replacing. If it's the extension lead's plug or one of its sockets, bin that extension lead. Don't use it for the dryer either, because a scorched lead is a fire risk.
2. Look at the part of the lead that was under the foot. Flattening, cuts, splits, or any coloured inner wire showing confirm the lead is damaged. Don't bend or handle it more than you need to.
3. Check the wall socket behind the dryer for any brown marks or melting. If you see any, the socket also needs an electrician. Whatever you find, the machine still needs testing before it's used. If the lead is damaged, an appliance engineer can fit a new mains lead and earth-test and insulation-test the machine in the same visit. That's usually a modest, worthwhile repair. The lead is wired inside the machine, so it isn't a DIY job. It's also worth asking an electrician to fit a separate socket for each appliance, somewhere you can reach, so they never need to share a lead again. Could you tell me which plug the scorch is on, and whether the trapped
its the extension lead plug thats scorched, near one of the pins. its the extension lead thats been trapped under the machines foot too, not the washers own cable i think

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That points quite strongly at the extension lead. A lead crushed under a machine's foot gets squashed and flexed on every spin, which can break the earth wire inside it. The scorching by one pin shows that connection has been overheating, very likely from carrying a washer and a dryer together. A broken earth explains the tingle exactly: the small leakage every washer has normally drains away through the earth, but with no earth it goes through you instead, more so when you're barefoot on tiles. In order, I'd now put it as:
1. The extension lead: lost earth from crushing, plus an overheating plug. This is the most likely cause.
2. The washer's own lead, plug or internal earth lead. This is less likely now, but not ruled out, especially as you're not completely sure which cable was trapped.
3. Leakage inside the machine, such as the heater. This is a distant possibility, and nothing tripping fits that being less likely. That extension lead is finished. Don't use it again for anything, including the dryer, because a scorched plug is a fire risk on its own. With everything unplugged and wearing shoes, two things are worth a look:
1. Run your eye along the washer's own cable and its plug, especially anywhere near the feet. Flattening, splits or scorching would mean its lead needs replacing too. If it looks perfect, that supports the extension lead being the whole story.
2. Check the wall socket behind the dryer for brown marks or melting. An overheating plug can damage the socket it sits in. Any marks there mean an electrician needs to look at it. We can't tell from looking whether the machine's own earth is sound, or whether that overheating has affected anything. An appliance engineer can do that test quickly and replace the machine's lead at the same visit if needed. It's also well worth getting an electrician to fit separate, reachable sockets for the washer and dryer, so they never have to share a lead again. washers own cable looks fine i think, not checked the wall socket properly as its behind the dryer. ok i'll leave it all unplugged till its looked at, need the kids uniforms done though

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Leaving it all unplugged is the right call. With the washer's own cable looking fine, the crushed and scorched extension lead is still the most likely cause. But only a proper earth and insulation test can confirm the machine itself is sound, so it stays off until it's been checked. For the uniforms, a few ways to get through the next day or two:
1. A launderette, or a family member or neighbour's machine. Many launderettes also do a cheap same-day service wash if you can't wait around.
2. Hand washing. Polo shirts, sweatshirts and socks clean up fine in a sink or bowl of warm water with a little detergent. Squeeze rather than wring, roll them in a towel to get most of the water out, and hang them on an airer or over a radiator overnight. Polycotton school polos usually dry by morning.
3. Spot-cleaning. Trousers and skirts can often go another day with a sponge and a damp cloth on the marks. Please don't use the dryer either for now. Its usual extension lead is the scorched one, and nobody has looked at the wall socket behind it yet. When the dryer is next pulled out, with everything switched off and unplugged, have a look at that socket. Any brown marks or melting mean an electrician needs to see it before anything goes back in. To get washing again quickly, book both visits now, and mention the tingle and scorching when you do, as some will prioritise it. An appliance engineer can earth- and insulation-test the washer. An electrician can check that socket and ideally fit a separate, reachable socket for each machine. If the test suggests it was just the extension lead, it's likely to be a quick, inexpensive visit and you'll be back up and running.
